title: The binary search bug that survived for years

segments.text: Binary search is the first algorithm a lot of us learn, and it still trips up experienced engineers.
The idea is simple: in a sorted array, check the middle element and throw away half the range each step.
That gives you logarithmic time, so a billion elements takes about thirty comparisons.
Here's the classic implementation: low starts at zero, high at the last index, and mid is low plus high divided by two.
And that last line has a bug that sat in a famous standard library for close to a decade.
When low and high are both large, low plus high can overflow a 32-bit integer.
The sum wraps around to a negative number and the program crashes or reads the wrong index.
The fix is to compute mid as low plus the difference between high and low, divided by two.
That version never exceeds high, so it can't overflow.
The second classic bug is the loop condition. Is it low less than high, or less than or equal?
Mixing the two with the wrong update rule gives you an infinite loop on two-element ranges.
My advice: pick one convention, write down the invariant, and test the edge cases.
Test an empty array, one element, two elements, the target at both ends, and a missing target.
Property-based testing is great here: compare your function against a simple linear scan on random inputs.
Finally, in Python you rarely need to write it yourself. The bisect module already does it correctly.
So: watch the overflow, be consistent with your bounds, and test the edges.

facts.fact: Binary search halves the range each step for log time
